title: Claude was trained on protein sequences at scale
lede: Xinming Tu tested frontier models on predicting the next amino acid in little-studied bacterial proteins and found only the latest Claude models can, evidence they saw protein sequences at scale in training.

points: The test uses 668 proteins from 167 Pfam families of unknown function, each compared against a shuffled copy to isolate knowledge of order.
Fable 5.2 gets 54% right on real sequences and 9% on shuffled ones; GPT, Gemini and seven open-weight models stay near zero.
Fable 5.2 beats every open protein language model tested, and Opus 5.5 is level with ProtGPT3-10B.
Accuracy rises with family size, holds in families with no papers, and carries over to proteins published after the training cutoff.
Opus 5.5 predicts human and mouse coding DNA but not the rest of the genome, so what it learned is proteins, not genomes.

points.text: One thread asks whether protein data, like code before it, could improve models well outside biology.
Several question the shuffled control, asking what counts as a correct prediction for a sequence that never occurs in nature.
Some say Claude's biosecurity filters already block routine work in the field, and expect gated access for accredited users.
Another hopes the skill is emergent from understanding chemistry rather than the result of explicit training.
